One press gives exactly two pulses: a copper bulb notices the press, and a short delay plus a second observer turn that one event into two blips. Detail: the bulb toggles on each rising edge, its comparator changes, an observer makes that a 2 tick pulse, a delay-3 repeater stretches it to 6 ticks, and a second observer pulses on both of the repeater's edges

One press gives exactly three pulses: the two-pulse bulb burst plus one more observer stage that adds a third blip. Detail: bulb, comparator, observer, delay-3 repeater, observer, then an observer watching the second observer toggles a second bulb whose own observers add the third pulse

One press gives exactly four pulses: one detected press is split into four copies that arrive at different times, like echoes, all into the same output. Detail: a bulb edge detector (bulb, comparator, observer) whose pulse fans out through observers, a second bulb and a torch into four delayed taps; any input length

While the input is held on, two observers stare at each other and keep firing, a pulse every 4 ticks; it stops when the input goes off. Detail: 3 blocks: the input extends a sticky piston that pushes one observer face to face with the other (the chase), and retracting it breaks the pair apart

One press gives exactly 2 pulses: the press holds two observers face to face for a fixed moment, and they fire at each other 2 times before being pulled apart. Detail: a bulb edge detector (bulb, comparator, observer) and a repeater hold a sticky piston out for a fixed time; the piston pushes an observer face to face with another and they chase (a pulse every 4 ticks) until it retracts

Lights the output only after the input has stayed on for 10 ticks, and turns it off the moment the input stops: the input reaches the output only through a stone that a sticky piston slides into place after a repeater delay, so short pulses never get through. Details: the input's dust points into the empty cell beside the output; a delay-3 repeater (6 ticks) and two dust power the sticky piston, so an input shorter than the repeater delay plus the piston's travel never lights the output. The repeater makes every piston pulse at least 4 ticks, so the piston never spits its stone.

Details: 5 dust carry the second comparator's output back to the first, losing 4 signal strength per 4-tick lap; while the input is on it keeps the loop full; the comparator the output reads sets the exact length.

Gives a 12-tick output pulse after each input pulse, and a new input restarts the 12 ticks: every input refills a small two-comparator loop that fades out on its own. Unlike an item timer, a 2-tick press gives the whole length, in 2-tick steps, with no items to load back. Details: a copper bulb, a comparator and two observers turn each rising edge into 4 ticks of full-strength signal for the loop; 6 dust carry the signal back around, losing 5 per 4-tick lap. A short pulse needs a lossier, longer return line, which is why the short versions take more blocks than the long ones.

Keeps the output on for 108 ticks after the input turns off (a long off-delay): a small fast loop keeps a bigger, slower loop topped up, and once the input is gone the big loop counts down; each extra pair of comparators in the big loop adds 56 ticks. Details: stage 1 is a two-comparator loop (4-tick lap) that the input holds full; once the input stops it decays 2 per lap, so its output lasts at least 28 ticks. A repeater reading it powers stage 2, a three-comparator loop (6-tick lap) that loses only 1 per lap; stage 1's long output refills it evenly at full strength, and once stage 1 dies stage 2 counts its 15 levels down and the output goes dark at 0. Why not an item timer (a hopper draining k items at 8 ticks each, about 6 blocks for any length): the items move back only one per 8 ticks too, so an item timer needs an input about as long as its delay before it can time again, and it only comes in 8-tick steps; this loop refills in 3 ticks of input and keeps 2-tick resolution. For delays of many seconds an item timer is the smaller build.

Gives a 116-tick output pulse after each input pulse, and a new input restarts it (a long retriggerable one-shot): each input fills a small fast loop that keeps a bigger, slower loop topped up, which then counts down; each extra pair of comparators in the big loop adds 56 ticks. Details: a copper bulb, a comparator and two observers turn each rising edge into 4 ticks of full-strength signal for stage 1, a two-comparator loop (4-tick lap) that decays 2 per lap, so its output lasts at least 28 ticks; a repeater reading it refills stage 2, a three-comparator loop (6-tick lap) that loses only 1 per lap, which then counts its 15 levels down. Why not an item timer (a hopper draining k items at 8 ticks each): refilling it takes about as long as the pulse itself, so a new input could not restart it at once; this one restarts on any 2-tick input. For one-shots of many seconds an item timer is the smaller build.

Gives one 14-tick output pulse per input pulse and ignores new inputs until it has finished: the input refills a small fading loop through a gate that the loop keeps shut while it runs. Unlike the hopper one-shot of the pulse study (8-tick steps, items to bring back before the next press), it times in 2-tick steps and is ready again a few ticks after its pulse. Details: a copper bulb, a comparator, an observer and a delay-3 repeater turn each rising edge into a 6-tick charge through a subtract comparator; the loop's own signal feeds that comparator's side, so edges during the pulse pass nothing; 6 dust return the signal, losing 5 per 4-tick lap (a short pulse needs a lossier, longer line, hence more blocks).

Gives one 118-tick output pulse per input pulse and ignores new inputs until it has finished (a long one-shot): the input fills a small fast loop through a gate, the small loop keeps a bigger slower loop topped up, and the big loop counts down while holding the gate shut; each extra pair of comparators in the big loop adds 56 ticks. Details: a copper bulb, a comparator, an observer and a delay-3 repeater charge stage 1 through a subtract comparator whose side is fed from between the two loops, so every edge is ignored until the output itself has ended; stage 2 is a three-comparator loop (6-tick lap) that loses only 1 per lap. Divides a fast clock by 3 (one output pulse for every 3 input pulses) and keeps up with clocks as fast as a pulse every 8 ticks, where the item-ring dividers stop at 10. Detail: three copper bulbs in a ring with exactly one lit; every input pulse passes the lit one on to the next (each step: the bulb's comparator gates a short edge pulse), and the output reads one of them

Turns a fast clock into a slow one: the output changes once every 3 input edges (on for 1.5 input pulses, off for 1.5), so it ticks 3 times slower with an even on/off split. Detail: a ring of 3 droppers passing one item around, one step per input edge (an observer fires it on both edges), and a copper bulb that flips each time the item comes back around; part of a family for any odd N

Keeps its output on for about 50 seconds (990 ticks) after the input turns off, in 6 blocks: two hoppers pass 125 cobblestone back and forth, and a comparator keeps the output on while the first hopper still holds any. It needs an input about as long as its delay to load the items back, one per 8 ticks; for short delays the comparator rings are better (they reload on a 2-tick input and keep 2-tick steps). Details: hopper A (facing east) and hopper B (facing west) face each other. The input block locks A while the input is on, and a torch on that block locks B while the input is off. So the input on pours B into A (8 ticks per item), and the input off lets A drain back into B (8 ticks per item). The comparator reads A: on as soon as A holds one item, off when A runs dry. Length: 8 ticks per item, here 125 items; a hopper holds up to 320 (about 2 minutes).

Gives 8 output pulses (2 ticks on, one every 4 ticks) for each input, and stays 25 blocks for any count: the count is the number of items in a dropper (5 items for 8 pulses, up to 579 pulses with 9 full stacks). Details: the input cell is a copper bulb; its comparator and an observer give one pulse per input rising edge, which toggles a second bulb on. The comparator reading that bulb locks the return hopper and powers a sticky piston that pushes an observer face to face with another, and the pair fires the dropper every 4 ticks, one item into the hopper each time; the other observer's back is the output. When the dropper is empty, its comparator turns off and the torch on its output block lights, toggling the bulb off: the piston pulls the observer away and the hopper returns the items, 8 ticks each.
